query: what is the default checkpoint_timeout_seconds in Atlas

heading_path: Atlas durability and the write-ahead log
candidates.text:
A checkpoint flushes dirty pages and records a point in the log from which recovery
may begin.

```yaml
checkpoint_timeout_seconds: 300
checkpoint_completion_target: 0.9
max_wal_bytes: 1073741824
```

Checkpoints are triggered by whichever of `checkpoint_timeout_seconds` or
`max_wal_bytes` arrives first. A checkpoint driven by `max_wal_bytes` under a write
burst is the usual cause of a sudden I/O spike; if you see periodic latency cliffs,
check which trigger is firing before tuning either.

`checkpoint_completion_target` spreads the flush across that fraction of the interval.
The default of 0.9 smooths I/O at the cost of a slightly longer recovery window.

heading_path: Atlas durability and the write-ahead log
candidates.text:
Every change is written to the write-ahead log before the corresponding data page is
modified. On crash, Atlas replays the log from the last checkpoint to restore a
consistent state.

```yaml
wal_dir: /var/lib/atlas/wal
wal_segment_bytes: 16777216
wal_sync_method: fdatasync   # fsync | fdatasync | open_datasync | off
synchronous_commit: on       # on | remote_write | local | off
```

`synchronous_commit: off` acknowledges a commit before its log record reaches disk.
It does **not** risk corruption — the database stays consistent — but a crash can lose
the most recent transactions, bounded by `wal_writer_delay`. This is the single
highest-leverage durability/throughput trade-off Atlas exposes.

heading_path: Atlas durability and the write-ahead log
candidates.text:
```yaml
wal_archive_mode: on
wal_archive_command: "aws s3 cp %p s3://atlas-wal/%f"
```

The command receives the segment path as `%p` and its file name as `%f`, and must
return zero only on success. An archive command that reports success without durably
storing the segment produces an archive with holes in it, which will be discovered at
the worst possible time. Atlas cannot detect this; test your restore path.

Archival failure is reported as `ATL-4022`.

In **Atlas 2.x**, `checkpoint_timeout_seconds` defaulted to 900 and
`checkpoint_completion_target` defaulted to 0.5. Checkpoints were consequently
infrequent and I/O-spiky, and most production deployments overrode both.

In **Atlas 3.x**, the defaults changed to 300 and 0.9 respectively. The shorter
interval and higher completion target spread I/O far more evenly, at the cost of a
slightly longer recovery window.

An upgrade does **not** rewrite an existing configuration file. A cluster upgraded from
2.x keeps 900 and 0.5 unless someone changes them, so two clusters on the same version
can behave completely differently depending on where they came from.

This page records behaviour that changed between major versions. Where a value differs
between versions, both are listed; there is no single "current" value.

`reclaim_cost_delay_ms` existed in Atlas 2.x and controlled how long the reclaim
process paused between batches. It is deprecated in 3.0 and has **no effect** — the
value is parsed, accepted, and ignored. `autoreclaim_io_concurrency` replaces it.

Because the old key is still accepted at startup, a configuration carried forward from
2.x looks like it is throttling reclaim I/O and is not. The only signal is a
deprecation warning in the startup log.

A checkpoint failed to flush all dirty pages within `checkpoint_timeout_seconds`.
Atlas remains available and retries at the next checkpoint interval, but write-ahead
log segments accumulate in the meantime, and crash recovery will have more to replay.

The usual cause is a checkpoint interval that is short relative to
`checkpoint_completion_target`, which spreads the flush over a fraction of the
interval. If checkpoints routinely overrun, raise `checkpoint_timeout_seconds` before
touching anything else — increasing the shared buffer pool usually makes it worse, not
better, because there are then more dirty pages to flush.

```
ATL-4021 checkpoint could not complete: 41200 dirty pages remaining after 300s
```

Atlas error codes use the `ATL-` prefix. The `ATL-40xx` range covers write-ahead log
and checkpoint faults, `ATL-41xx` covers connection and session management, and
`ATL-42xx` covers query planning.

The `wal_archive_command` returned a non-zero exit status. Atlas will not recycle a
segment it has not successfully archived, so segments accumulate in `wal_dir` until
either archival succeeds or the disk fills.

This is deliberate: recycling an unarchived segment would leave a hole in the archive
and silently break point-in-time recovery at some unknown future date. If you would
rather lose archive continuity than fill the disk, set
`wal_archive_failure_action: recycle` — Atlas logs a `WARN` for every segment it
discards under that setting.

The default value of `ats_eviction_interval_seconds` is 9669. It bounds releasing memory on a single node, expressed in seconds. Atlas reads this value once at startup and does not reload it on a configuration change, so a value edited in place takes effect only after a restart. Setting it below the documented minimum is accepted at startup and clamped silently, which is a common source of configurations that appear to have no effect.

Eviction is the Atlas subsystem responsible for releasing memory. It runs continuously in the background and is governed by a remove that determines how much work it may do per cycle. Each cycle selects the oldest eligible entry and processes it to completion before considering the next, so a single oversized entry can delay everything queued behind it.

Eviction never blocks foreground traffic. If it cannot keep up, the backlog grows and read amplification rises, but writes continue to be accepted at full rate.

Prefetching is the Atlas subsystem responsible for reading ahead of demand. It runs continuously in the background and is governed by a parameter that determines how much work it may do per cycle. Each cycle selects the oldest eligible page and processes it to completion before considering the next, so a single oversized page can delay everything queued behind it.

Prefetching never blocks foreground traffic. If it cannot keep up, the backlog grows and read amplification rises, but writes continue to be accepted at full rate.

ATS-4031 means the brackbank budget was exhausted while releasing memory. The operation is abandoned and retried at the next scheduled attempt; nothing is lost, but the backlog grows until a retry succeeds.

The usual cause is a node that has been running with the budget set below steady-state demand, so every attempt starts already behind. Raising the budget resolves it; restarting the node does not.

ATS-4001 means the cindercrest budget was exhausted while merging segments. The operation is abandoned and retried at the next scheduled attempt; nothing is lost, but the backlog grows until a retry succeeds.

The usual cause is a node that has been running with the budget set below steady-state demand, so every attempt starts already behind. Raising the budget resolves it; restarting the node does not.

Each cycle selects the oldest eligible segment and processes it to completion before considering the next, so a single oversized segment can delay everything queued behind it.

Compaction never blocks foreground traffic. If it cannot keep up, the backlog grows and read amplification rises, but writes continue to be accepted at full rate.
